session_title: Initial Exploration and Visual Pre-assessment of the Restaurant
theme: 饮食-争议餐厅的美学考察

content.text: Gu Yanci, I just received the official promotional photos of this new restaurant. Take a look at the interior design. The combination of concrete walls and wooden seating, with light streaming in from the skylight, creates a very serene atmosphere overall. What do you think?

Hmm, I clicked and took a look. The rough texture of the concrete and the warmth of the wood create an interesting dialogue, but the way the black surface of the metal table reflects light feels a bit harsh, disrupting the overall harmony. The design feels too deliberate—are you sure it's not just formalism?

Haha, I knew you'd say that! But look at the lighting design—doesn't it resemble the stage of a modern art installation? I think it’s very narrative and guides the viewer’s gaze. You’ve always criticized me for focusing too much on visuals, so this time, I specifically wanted to hear your 'visual audit.'

Narrative? Don't use that artsy tone. The play of light and shadow does have layers, but the position of the skylight might make the midday light too harsh, affecting the dining experience. Design should serve function, not the other way around. Are you sending this to invite me for an on-site visit?

Exactly! I also took photos of the details of their tableware. Look at this heart-shaped plate, white with a gold rim, and the way they're stacked is quite intricate. But I feel the asymmetrical design is a bit forced. You mentioned before that form should serve function—could this be overshadowing the main purpose?

The glaze on the tableware has a nice texture, and the gold trim adds a touch of luxury, but the heart shape is too cliché and lacks innovation. Additionally, while the stacking method is visually appealing, it may compromise practicality—could it easily slip? The design ethics of this restaurant are questionable.

I agree with the point about practicality. However, as a visual content curator, I appreciate this cross-media dialogue—concrete, metal, and ceramics all tell a story. Do you think if we were to experience it, it would be a visual feast or a waste of money?

Wasting money? That depends on the food itself. But since you asked, I can accept the invitation, though I’m going for an "on-site visual audit, not just a meal." You’d better be prepared for my sharp-tongued comments and not get upset like last time when I criticized you.

Don't worry, I'm used to your sarcasm! Look at the plating of their dishes—it's molecular gastronomy style, and the color combinations are quite artistic. But I feel this strong stylization might overshadow the taste of the food. You’ve always emphasized the democratization of aesthetics—does this count as over-design?

Overdesigned? Absolutely! The plating is too flashy, like showing off skills rather than enhancing the experience. The color contrast is strong, but it lacks unity, making it visually chaotic. The restaurant's designer may have forgotten that beauty lies in the details, but the details should not overwhelm the whole.

You're right, details are important. I noticed how the interplay of light and shadow with the plating could create a unique atmosphere. But if we go, what would you focus on—the spatial layout or the design of the tableware?

Both are important. The spatial layout affects the flow and comfort, while the design of the tableware reflects the brand's values. However, I'm more concerned about the font on the menu—you've shared similar issues before. If the readability is poor, then the design fails. Do you have any pictures of the menu?

Yes, I just found the menu. It has a retro hand-drawn style with highly decorative fonts, but it might sacrifice some clarity. Do you think this aligns with the concept of "visuals as storytelling," or is it purely for aesthetics?

The font choice 'sacrifices readability in the pursuit of being overly avant-garde,' as I directly quoted from your earlier summary. The hand-drawn illustrations are creative, but the core purpose of a menu is to convey information, not to serve as an art exhibition. The overall design of this restaurant seems to have misplaced its priorities.
I agree with your criticism. So, shall we set a time to go? With the purpose of critical observation, perhaps we could write a joint review to share with readers. What do you think?

Sure, but don't expect me to go easy. I'll conduct a comprehensive evaluation from the perspectives of visual order and design ethics. You decide the time, and send me the location. Remember, this is an aesthetic review, not a culinary tour.

Alright, Master Gu! I look forward to your 'audit report.' Perhaps this collaboration will help us better understand each other's professional perspectives—you focus on form, I focus on narrative, but both of us pursue beauty in the details.
Don't call me a master, it's too cheesy. But you're right, our core values intersect: visual order and everyday poetry can coexist. Consider this visit as a test of that hypothesis.
Haha, deal! I'll send you the specific details. Thanks for your sharp tongue—it always makes me think deeper. See you later!
Yeah, see you later. Remember to bring your camera to document the 'evidence of the crime'.
